title: The Morning Brief: Envoys in Moscow as Ukraine bleeds; Pentagon fires journalists
dek: U.S. peace envoys arrived in Moscow on Saturday carrying an undisclosed proposal to end the Ukraine conflict as Russia announced a three-day capital ceasefire, yet Russian attacks continued overnight, killing at least five civilians. Separately, a federal judge cleared the Pentagon to fire three Stars and Stripes journalists after their CBS News interviews, and military experts called a polygraph sweep of 50 Joint Staff members unprecedented in scope.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The gap between announced pause and continued violence defines today's picture: peace talks begin while both sides test the ceasefire's durability, and the Trump administration tightens control over defense reporting at the same moment it pursues diplomatic settlement.
bottom_line: Peace envoys began talks in Moscow on Saturday while Russian forces continued attacks overnight, signaling the ceasefire's fragility before negotiations formally open. The Pentagon simultaneously blocked journalists from reporting on military conditions and polygraphed 50 Joint Staff members in what experts called an unprecedented leak probe, a tightening of information control that occurs as the administration pursues diplomatic settlement. The U.S. also escalated strikes on Iranian economic infrastructure after Iranian missile attacks on Navy ships. Watch Monday for the envoys' first visit to Kyiv and their initial readout; watch whether the three-day capital-city ceasefire holds through September 8; and watch the next Iranian response and its effect on oil markets.
body: U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday, September 5, carrying what President Trump described as a fresh proposal to end the five-year Ukraine conflict. Russian state media reported that President Vladimir Putin ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv for three days, and Ukraine's military was ordered to cease fire for the same period starting at midnight Saturday through September 8. Yet within hours, the announced pause fractured: Russian forces attacked the city of Kamianske in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region, killing at least five people and injuring five others. Russian strikes also targeted Kyiv's airports overnight, which President Zelenskyy characterized as a demonstration against the envoys' expected arrival in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday. Ukraine's air force reported Russia launched 167 attack drones overnight and deployed increasingly lethal jet-powered drones that fly at about half the speed of a passenger jet, making them harder to intercept. Ukrainian air defenses suppressed or shot down 128 of the drones. The envoys' travel route from Moscow to Kyiv remained unresolved as of Sunday morning, since Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

On the domestic reporting front, a federal judge on Friday denied a restraining order that would have blocked the Pentagon from firing three Stars and Stripes journalists: publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte. U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ruled that the government likely did not violate the First Amendment rights of the employees, who had given interviews to CBS News in July and whose employer published a story on August 11 detailing mental health concerns and food and water shortages aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. The judge found that Slavin and Korte gave their CBS interviews in their capacity as Stars and Stripes employees, not as private citizens, and noted they had toed the company line. The Pentagon stated the termination process began more than a month before the Abraham Lincoln story ran. Two additional lawsuits against the Pentagon remain pending, one filed by Pulitzer-winning reporters Susan Dardarian and William Church in June, and another by former ombudsman Jacqueline Smith, also in June, as discovery and potential trial continue.

The Pentagon also launched what legal and military experts describe as an unprecedented leak investigation, subjecting approximately 50 members of the Joint Staff to polygraph tests last month. The inquiry targeted disclosure of classified information about dwindling U.S. ammunition reserves and operations involving Iran. News outlets published reports last month highlighting severe drops in long-range missiles and Patriot air defense interceptors; U.S. officials pushed back on those claims. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell stated the department investigates leaks "extremely seriously," citing the criticality of securing classified information. The investigation has not yet produced public evidence of identified suspects or personnel actions, and the legal authority for administering the tests and their binding status remain unaddressed.

Elsewhere on the diplomatic front, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee visited the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya on Saturday and called ongoing settler violence an "act of terror." He met with approximately 10 Palestinian American residents describing property damage, mosque burning, and home invasions, stating the conduct "extends beyond a criminal act." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu characterized the violence as acts of a "handful of rioters," signaling the Israeli government will not adopt the U.S. framing. Settler attacks against Palestinians exceeded 1,800 incidents in 2025, according to the United Nations. The Israeli government has built nearly 150 settlements home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers in the West Bank.

In the Persian Gulf, U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday in retaliation after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy ships. No American personnel were harmed in the Iranian attacks. U.S. forces permanently disabled two crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and destroyed a third vessel, the M/T Kylo, near the Gulf of Oman. The Kylo's crew was evacuated before the strike. The action marks a shift from military-to-military targeting toward deliberate damage to Iran's economic infrastructure.

On domestic economic data, the U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs in August 2026, exceeding economist expectations of at least 50,000 new jobs, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, down from a peak of 4.5% in November 2025. Private companies, however, added only 38,000 jobs, the lowest monthly gain since January. Manufacturing added 16,000 jobs in July, the strongest gain in three years, while leisure and hospitality saw the strongest gains in August. Annual inflation went from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stated at Jackson Hole that "we must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do." Trump celebrated the August figures and threatened to halt trading with countries running deficits with the U.S. if the Fed does not lower interest rates.

A volcanic eruption of Mount Anak Krakatau forced Indonesia to temporarily suspend operations at eight airports on Sunday, stranding more than 150,000 passengers and disrupting 712 flights. Volcanic ash reached altitudes of up to 50,000 feet. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was the first to close after ash was detected in nearby airspace. By mid-afternoon local time, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 at Jakarta's hub alone affecting about 22,800 passengers. No casualties were reported and no evacuation orders were issued, as the nearest settlement is more than 10 miles away, though residents in ash-affected areas faced respiratory, eye, and skin risks.

Finally, the Supreme Court agreed to hear cases challenging rifle bans imposed by Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. The central question is whether the Second Amendment protects the right to possess AR-15-style and similar semiautomatic rifles. A dozen states have enacted such bans. Americans own over 30 million of these rifles, commonly for self-defense, hunting, and target shooting. The Court's decision will turn on how justices apply the historical test established in Bruen to firearms manufactured after 1868.
